checkpoints: Translate "lose at most half an hour of the most recent orders" into RPO = 30 minutes (the maximum data loss allowed, measured from the last backup/checkpoint to the incident).
Translate "back up within 1 hour" into RTO = 1 hour (the maximum downtime allowed before the system is fully recovered).

State the core principle that the gap between two consecutive backups/checkpoints must be ≤ the RPO, because with sparser backups an incident can land right after a backup and right before the next one, losing more than the target amount of data.
Propose the minimum backup frequency of every 30 minutes as the baseline needed to just satisfy the 30-minute RPO.

Recommend a safety margin beyond the bare minimum: go tighter than 30 minutes (e.g. every 15-20 minutes) to absorb timing slack, or — for a critical database like orders — replace discrete backups with a continuous mechanism such as point-in-time recovery (PITR) via continuous WAL/binlog shipping for a near-zero RPO.

Explain why backing up every 24 hours is completely inadequate: an incident right before the next scheduled backup could lose nearly 24 hours of data, roughly 48 times over the 30-minute RPO requirement, a severe violation.

Note that the 1-hour RTO is a separate constraint from backup frequency — frequent backups alone don't guarantee a fast restore; a practiced (ideally automated) restore process/drills is needed to ensure the system is actually back up within 1 hour, rather than assuming the restore will be fast.
Disagree — "the whole system is backed up" is a wrong and dangerous conclusion.
Velero DOES capture every Kubernetes object in the namespace (Deployment, ConfigMap, Secret, the StatefulSet definition) as YAML manifests backed up into object storage.
Velero DOES capture the PVC attached to the in-cluster Postgres (StatefulSet) via a VolumeSnapshot — assuming the CSI driver is correctly configured to support snapshots — so that data is restorable.

Velero does NOT capture RDS: it runs entirely outside the Kubernetes cluster and is not a Kubernetes object, with no corresponding PersistentVolume/PersistentVolumeClaim inside the cluster — so Velero has zero visibility into or ability to touch RDS data.

This gap is serious because the main user data in RDS — often the most valuable, most critical part of the whole system — is not under Velero's protection at all, so an RDS incident would reveal the "backup" never covered the most important part.
The fix: RDS needs its own backup mechanism independent of Velero, e.g. AWS RDS automated backups/manual snapshots (point-in-time recovery) or periodic pg_dump/logical backups for finer control.
A complete DR strategy must coordinate BOTH Velero (for what runs in-cluster) and the managed service's own backup mechanism (for what runs outside the cluster).
It must also restore-test both parts together to confirm the system can be fully recovered — not just half of it.

Every plain Kubernetes object in the namespace — ConfigMap `app-config`, Secret `db-credentials`, Deployment `orders-api`, and the StatefulSet `orders-db` definition — backed up SUCCESSFULLY (the "configuration" part).
The PersistentVolumeClaim `orders-db-pvc-0` backup FAILED (no snapshot taken) — this is the failed part.

The exact root cause is the error `"no volumesnapshotclass found for provisioner ebs.csi.aws.com"`: the cluster has no `VolumeSnapshotClass` matching the CSI provisioner `ebs.csi.aws.com` that the `fast-ssd` storage class uses.

Mechanism: Velero needs a matching `VolumeSnapshotClass` to know which snapshot API to call for that provisioner; without one it silently SKIPS the volume rather than hard-failing the whole backup — which is exactly why the overall status reads `PartiallyFailed` instead of `Failed`.

The "PartiallyFailed = no big deal" conclusion is dangerous because the failed PVC is exactly the volume holding ALL of the `orders-db` database's data — the most valuable resource in the namespace, not a peripheral one.

If restored from this backup after a real incident, the Deployment/ConfigMap/Secret and the `orders-db` pod would come back and start up fine, but the data inside would be completely empty since no snapshot was ever taken — a system that looks like it's working but is actually empty of data.

The fix is to create (or verify) a `VolumeSnapshotClass` with `driver: ebs.csi.aws.com` matching `fast-ssd`'s provisioner exactly, attaching the `velero.io/csi-volumesnapshot-class: "true"` label if Velero requires it to identify the correct class.

After the fix, rerun the backup and confirm via `velero backup describe` that `Phase: Completed` and `orders-db-pvc-0` now shows a successfully created `VolumeSnapshot` instead of "no snapshot taken".

Identify snapshotVolumes: false as the most dangerous/serious issue and explain that it is a deliberate choice (per the comment) whose real consequence the author missed: it completely disables volume snapshotting for every PersistentVolumeClaim in the namespace.

Explain the silent-failure trap concretely: if prod-orders has an in-cluster database (a PVC attached to a StatefulSet), the backup would only save manifests (Deployment/ConfigMap/Secret) with no volume snapshot at all, yet `velero backup describe` would still report `Phase: Completed`, making it look fine while being useless for restoring real data.

Identify schedule: "0 2 * * *" as only running once per day, creating a ~24-hour gap between backups that violates the 30-minute RPO requirement (up to ~24h of data loss, about 48x over the allowed threshold).
Identify ttl: 24h0m0s as only retaining each backup for 24 hours before Velero garbage-collects it, violating the compliance requirement to keep at least 30 days of backup history.
Prescribe the fix for snapshotVolumes: set it to true (or remove it entirely, since true is Velero's default).
Prescribe the fix for schedule: change it to run every 30 minutes (e.g. cron */30 * * * *) to match the RPO requirement.
Prescribe the fix for ttl: set it to at least 720h0m0s (30 days) to satisfy the compliance retention requirement.

Recommend post-fix verification: run a test backup, use `velero backup describe --details` to confirm the PVC has a successful VolumeSnapshot, and perform a test restore to confirm real data comes back — rather than trusting `Phase: Completed` alone.

Backup-restore cannot meet a 30-minute RTO because most of the measured 4-hour failover time comes from building the entire infrastructure from scratch (creating a new cluster from IaC, waiting for nodes to boot, configuring networking) rather than from slow data restore, since backup + WAL shipping already give a fine ~15-minute RPO.
This from-scratch provisioning delay is an inherent core limitation of the lowest DR tier, not a configuration bug fixable by optimizing the backup mechanism itself.

The recommended move is to jump to the next tier: pilot light — keeping a minimal copy of the core infrastructure already running in the secondary region (a database replica that is actually running and continuously receiving WAL/binlog to stay near-synchronized, plus core networking/VPC already configured), while compute/service capacity is kept at a minimum or entirely off.

On failover with pilot light, you only need to scale up the compute/service layer (add replicas, start the application) on top of an already-ready core, instead of building the entire infrastructure from scratch, cutting out most of the provisioning time that dominated the previous 4-hour measurement.

There is no need to jump straight to warm standby or multi-site active-active, because pilot light is usually enough to reach an RTO of a few dozen minutes — matching the 30-minute requirement — while costing significantly less than those two higher, more expensive tiers.

Tier selection principle: cost increases and RTO decreases along backup-restore → pilot light → warm standby → multi-site active-active, so the right approach is to pick the lowest tier that just meets the actual RTO needed rather than over-provisioning to the most expensive tier "to be safe" when a near-zero RTO isn't actually required.

After deploying pilot light, it is mandatory to run a real restore/failover drill on an environment close to production to measure the actual RTO, confirming it is truly under 30 minutes before reporting to the business that the requirement is met.

Hook được đính kèm qua ANNOTATION trên chính POD `orders-db-0` (không phải trên Schedule/Backup object), vì Velero cần biết chính xác pod nào + container nào để chạy lệnh trước khi snapshot volume của pod đó.

`Schedule` object cấu hình đúng 3 field cơ bản: `schedule: "*/30 * * * *"` chạy mỗi 30 phút khớp RPO; `ttl: 720h0m0s` (30 ngày x 24h) giữ đủ lịch sử, Velero tự garbage-collect backup cũ hơn mốc này; `snapshotVolumes: true` đảm bảo mọi PVC trong namespace `prod-orders` đều được snapshot đầy đủ, không bỏ sót data.
`pre.hook.backup.velero.io/container: postgres` chỉ định đúng container chạy lệnh trong pod `orders-db-0`, tránh chạy nhầm sang sidecar khác nếu pod có nhiều container.

`pre.hook.backup.velero.io/command` chạy `psql -c "CHECKPOINT;"` như một PRE-hook — Velero đảm bảo lệnh chạy XONG rồi mới bắt đầu snapshot volume; `/timeout` giới hạn thời gian Velero chờ hook hoàn tất, tránh treo vô hạn nếu DB không phản hồi.

Volume snapshot chỉ chụp trạng thái các DISK BLOCK tại một thời điểm — không có nhận thức về ngữ nghĩa của Postgres đang chạy bên trên; Postgres giữ các thay đổi đã commit trong WAL buffer/memory cache, chỉ tự flush xuống đĩa theo chu kỳ checkpoint riêng của nó.

Nếu snapshot được chụp giữa hai lần checkpoint, dữ liệu trên đĩa có thể chỉ ở trạng thái crash-consistent (giống mất điện đột ngột — Postgres tự phục hồi được qua WAL replay khi khởi động lại) nhưng KHÔNG đảm bảo phản ánh đầy đủ các transaction vừa commit gần nhất, và trong tình huống phức tạp có thể cần thời gian phục hồi lâu hơn hoặc mang rủi ro không mong muốn.

Lệnh `CHECKPOINT` buộc Postgres FLUSH NGAY LẬP TỨC toàn bộ dữ liệu đã commit từ memory xuống đĩa trước khi hook kết thúc, đảm bảo tại thời điểm Velero bắt đầu snapshot, trạng thái trên đĩa phản ánh bức tranh đầy đủ và chính xác nhất, giảm thiểu rủi ro khi restore.

Explains the minimum storage duration charge concept: every storage class cheaper than Standard carries a mandatory minimum storage time (Standard-IA 30 days, Glacier Instant/Flexible Retrieval 90 days, Deep Archive 180 days).
Explains that deleting an object earlier than its class's minimum still incurs charges for the full minimum duration as if it had sat there the whole time — early deletion does not save money.

Applies this to the log scenario: because the team deletes app logs after just a few days (far shorter than Deep Archive's 180-day minimum), forcing all objects including these logs into Deep Archive after 1 day makes the actual cost HIGHER than leaving them in Standard and deleting on schedule.

Points out the retrieval cost/latency tradeoff: retrieval cost runs inversely to storage cost, so cheaper storage classes like Deep Archive are more expensive and slower to retrieve from (12-48 hours), which hurts if logs occasionally need to be pulled for debugging.
States the correct rule: only transition an object to a storage class when its expected lifetime is greater than or equal to that class's minimum duration.

Recommends that short-lived data like logs stay in Standard storage and use expiration (not transition) rules to delete on schedule, while only data genuinely needing long-term retention (audit trails, compliance backups, legal data) is worth transitioning to Glacier/Deep Archive.
Recommends segmenting lifecycle rules by filter.prefix (e.g. separating log types) instead of applying one blanket rule to every object in the bucket.
Disagrees with the teammate's claim — Multi-AZ and Read Replica solve two completely different problems, even though both involve "replication".

Multi-AZ uses synchronous replication: the primary only acknowledges a commit after the standby (in a different AZ, same region) has written the data — giving RPO = 0 and RTO of about 30 seconds; the standby receives no application traffic at all, it just waits to take over on failover.

Read Replica uses asynchronous replication: the replica can be in the same AZ or cross-region and DOES receive real read traffic from the application, enabling horizontal read scaling; because it's async, RPO is > 0 due to replication lag (milliseconds to a few seconds).

The two mechanisms serve independent purposes: Multi-AZ solves the high-availability problem (surviving an AZ outage without data loss, automatic failover), while Read Replica solves the scale-out read-traffic problem (offloading the primary as read volume grows).

They are not substitutes for each other: Multi-AZ alone still piles all read traffic onto a single primary despite having a standby ready; Read Replica alone means an AZ outage can take down write capability, requiring manual promotion or accepting longer downtime.

This is exactly why production setups usually need BOTH — Multi-AZ for high availability/failover and Read Replica for read scaling — directly rebutting the teammate's claim that Multi-AZ alone makes a read replica unnecessary.
Aurora merges both concepts: its reader endpoint both serves read traffic like a read replica and can be promoted to writer on failover, resembling a Multi-AZ standby but more flexible.
This is a hot partition problem: every write uses the exact same partition key `GLOBAL_COUNTER`.

DynamoDB hashes the PK to route requests to a physical partition, so an identical PK on every write funnels ALL traffic into a single partition while the table's other partitions sit completely empty.

On-demand mode doesn't prevent this because DynamoDB's throughput limits (~3000 RCU / 1000 WCU) apply at the physical partition level, not the whole-table level — so a single overloaded partition gets throttled even while the table's aggregate capacity still has headroom, matching the observed symptom.

The root cause is PK cardinality being far too low: DynamoDB needs high PK cardinality (recommended ≥1000 unique values per 1M items) to spread traffic across many physical partitions, but this PK has only one value for the entire system-wide counter.
The fix is write sharding: change the PK to `GLOBAL_COUNTER#shard-N` with N a random number (e.g. 0-9), raising cardinality so writes distribute across multiple partitions instead of one.
To read the total counter value, the application must Query/aggregate across all shards and sum the results.

DynamoDB's Adaptive Capacity can auto-rebalance traffic to other partitions, but it takes minutes to kick in, so it won't save a short burst at peak hours — proactive write sharding is still the solution rather than relying on the system to self-heal.
